Results and discussion 3.1. Performance analysis of fusion strategies To comprehensively evaluate the impact of multimodal fusion strate- gies on seedling stress classification, we conducted comparative exper- iments on three network configurations: RGB-CTA, RGBD-CTA-D, and RGBD-CTA-F. Quantitative results are reported in Table 3. The FPS was measured on Jetson AGX Xavier using native PyTorch FP32 inference with a batch parameter of 1. The timing was averaged over 100 test images and included image preprocessing and inference threads running in parallel with robotic arm, and gripper control programs. The performance metrics in Table 3 reveal the relative strengths of the three fusion strategies in terms of both overall correctness and class- level discriminability. RGB-CTA sets the baseline with a balanced yet restricted performance across all four metrics. This outcome reflects the information bottleneck that is intrinsically present in the single-modal RGB representation when differentiating subtle stress variations. The marginal improvements of RGBD-CTA-D over RGB-CTA indicate that simply appending depth as an extra channel offers limited complemen- tary signals. It gives some noise reduction or contextual help but lacks an explicit way to integrate modality-specific semantics. In comparison with the baseline model, RGBD-CTA-F achieves approximately 5 % improvements in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These en- hancements serve to validate the effectiveness of cross-attention-based feature-level fusion. By leveraging the complementary cues of RGB appearance and depth geometry, the network can more dependably dis- tinguish subtle seedling stress patterns (Sun et al., 2022). The consistent precision and recall improvement indicates that RGBD-CTA-F enhances positive identification accuracy. It also improves the comprehensive- ness of detecting stressed classes, thereby increasing the F1-Score. It is crucial for fine-grained multiclass stress classification where both false positives and false negatives carry operational cost. Regarding computational efficiency and deployment feasibility, Ta- ble 3 reveals critical trade-offs between model complexity and perfor- mance. The RGB-CTA and RGBD-CTA-D models exhibit nearly identical parameter sizes (18.09 M vs. 18.35 M) and inference speeds (7.6 FPS vs. 7.4 FPS), reflecting their shared backbone architecture with only minor modifications to accommodate the depth channel. This finding indicates that merely adding depth as an additional input dimension incurs only a negligible computational burden. However, it also results in only minimal improvements in classification accuracy (from 90.9 % to 91.2 %). This observation underscores the restricted effectiveness of data-level fusion in harnessing multimodal synergy. By contrast, the RGBD-CTA-F model, with its dedicated dual-stream encoder and CA fusion module, increases the parameter count to 23.22 M and reduces the inference speed to 5.2 FPS. While this represents a 28 % increase in model size and a 31.5 % decrease in speed relative to the baseline, the performance gain is substantial—boosting accuracy from 90.9 % to 95.8 %. The dual-stream encoders and cross-attention fusion introduce additional parameters and computa- tion to better exploit complementary RGB and depth cues. Importantly, the model maintains a frame rate above the camera acquisition rate (5 FPS), ensuring it can process incoming frames in real time without introducing bottlenecks. From a computational perspective, giga floating-point operations (GFLOPs) provide a more direct measure of workload than parameter count alone. The GFLOPs increase from 8.2 (RGB-CTA) to 8.6 (RGBD- CTA-D) and further to 10.3 (RGBD-CTA-F). This trend is consistent with the architectural evolution from a single-stream backbone to a dual-stream design with cross-attention-based feature fusion. While RGBD-CTA-D introduces only a minor increase in computation by ex- panding the input channel, RGBD-CTA-F incorporates parallel RGB and depth encoders as well as cross-attention operations, which substan- tially increase matrix multiplications and memory access operations. The observed decrease in FPS is therefore primarily attributed to the higher computational complexity and increased memory bandwidth demand. In particular, cross-attention modules introduce additional tensor reshaping and attention score computation. Furthermore, given that the operating frequency of the transplant- ing robotic arm typically allows several hundred milliseconds for decision-making per seedling, the marginal latency introduced by RGBD-CTA-F is well within practical tolerances. These results indi- cate that the additional computational cost of feature-level fusion is acceptable, especially in precision agriculture scenarios where mis- classification of stressed seedlings can incur significant downstream losses. Since Table 3 cannot fully represent the predictions for each class, we further compared the performance of the three models using a con- fusion matrix, as shown in Fig. 9. According to the rules for plotting the confusion matrix, the numbers on the diagonal of each matrix (from the top-left to the bottom-right) represent the correct predictions for each class. The higher these numbers, the better the model’s performance for the respective class. We analyze the confusion matrix generated by the RGB-CTA model on the test dataset, as shown in Fig. 9a, as the baseline. The RGB-CTA model displays significant off-diagonal dispersion, particularly in intermediate stress categories (e.g., W4N0 vs. W4N4 and W6N0), suggesting difficulty in distinguishing subtle visual differences. The RGBD-CTA-D fusion approach treats depth and color equally, without according precedence to modality-specific semantics or dy- namic relevance. A more detailed analysis of the confusion matrix reveals that, compared with the RGB-CTA baseline, the variety of error types has increased, as shown in Fig. 9b. Consequently, this approach results in information dilution rather than augmentation. Specifically, several intermediate stress categories (such as W2N0- W4N0) exhibit more frequent cross-class confusions. This implies that the incorporated depth channel introduces ambiguities that cannot be effectively resolved by simple concatenation. This discovery suggests that naive data-level fusion may inadvertently intensify subtle inter- class overlaps when the modalities are not adaptively coordinated. Thus, it underscores the need for more structured fusion mechanisms to clarify correlated yet distinct stress signatures. In contrast, Fig. 9c reveals a predominantly diagonal distribution for RGBD-CTA-F, indicating the model’s capacity to differentiate stress levels with high confidence. By modeling RGB features as query vectors and depth features as keys and values, the network dynamically attends to spatial regions where structural deformation (e.g., curled leaves, com- pacted root systems) aligns with stress-induced discoloration, thereby enhancing class separability. A closer examination of the confusion matrices indicates that most misclassified samples are concentrated in intermediate stress cate- gories, such as W2N0, W4N4, and W4N0, where visual differences are subtle and class boundaries are inherently ambiguous. These hard-to- classify samples often share similar phenotypic characteristics, includ- ing slight chlorosis, moderate leaf shrinkage, and comparable canopy structure, making discrimination particularly challenging. In addition, variations in observation angle may cause partial leaf self-occlusion and canopy structure changes, occasionally masking discriminative symptoms such as localized chlorosis or wilted leaves. Moreover, forward–backward tilting of seedlings during robotic grasping can alter the camera-to-seedling distance, introducing inconsistencies in appar- ent scale that further increase classification ambiguity. RGBD-CTA-F reduces these confusions more effectively under occlusion and scale variation, indicating that cross-attention-based RGBD fusion improves robustness by jointly leveraging appearance and geometric cues. In summary, the feature-level fusion architecture with CA not only amplifies the synergistic benefits of RGB and depth data but also facilitates semantic alignment across modalities, leading to noticeably higher classification accuracy and reliability. This validates the pro- posed model as a viable solution for real-time stress grading in precision seedling transplantation systems. 3.2. Interpretability via Grad-CAM attention maps To further evaluate the interpretability and visual reasoning ca- pabilities of the proposed models, we employed gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) (Selvaraju et al., 2016) to gen- erate class-discriminative localization maps. These visualizations help identify salient regions within the input image that contribute most significantly to the model’s final prediction, thereby revealing the internal focus mechanism of different architectures. Fig. 10 illustrates a series of Grad-CAM visualizations for ran- dom sample seedlings, highlighting the attention regions across differ- ent network variants. Warmer colors (e.g., red) indicate regions with higher contributions to the classification output, whereas cooler colors (e.g., blue) represent less influential or redundant areas. For each ex- ample, the predicted stress category and the corresponding confidence score are explicitly annotated, providing a direct visualization of the six-level stress classification outcome. From the results in Fig. 10b, it is evident that the RGB-CTA model often concentrates on localized features such as root boundaries or individual leaves. These attention areas are narrow and fragmented. Although they occasionally align with stress indicators, they often fail to capture broader contextual or structural cues. This phenomenon accounts for the model’s confusion at intermediate stress levels. The heatmaps also reveal that important areas, such as subtle chlorosis on multiple leaves or combined morphology cues, are not consistently aggregated. This results in unstable decision regions. The RGBD-CTA-D variant in Fig. 10c shows more spatially extended attention compared to RGB-CTA, suggesting that the addition of depth information does help broaden the receptive focus. However, the at- tention is still irregular and exhibits scattered high-response patches that do not form semantically coherent regions. Further, it can be noted that the dispersed high-response patches did not effectively concentrate on the cues. This partial integration leads to an inconsistent weighting of appearance and geometric features. This phenomenon is manifested as both redundant and insufficient emphasis, which contributes to the heightened confusion among similar stress categories, as previously noted and as shown in Fig. 9b. In contrast, the RGBD-CTA-F model Fig. 10d, which utilizes a CA- based feature fusion mechanism, demonstrates enhanced spatial aware- ness. Its attention regions are more uniformly distributed over seman- tically rich parts of the seedling, including leaf clusters, root collars, and inter-leaf spaces. Such patterns align closely with human-perceived stress indicators like leaf chlorosis, growth asymmetry, and shoot vigor. This suggests that the model is not only learning more relevant features but also reasoning more effectively by leveraging the complementary information from RGB and depth modalities. Overall, the attention visualizations not only support the quantita- tive performance gains observed in previous sections but also demon- strate that the RGBD-CTA-F model exhibits satisfactory interpretabil- ity. This property is important for real-world agricultural deployment, where model transparency and trustworthiness are essential for user adoption and decision-making under variable field conditions. 3.3. Ablation study: Impact of fusion direction in CA module In the design of the CA module, we selected RGB features as the query (primary feature) and depth features as the key and value (reference features). This is a common and effective design pattern in multimodal learning. This pattern allows the model to leverage depth features to enhance and complement the information provided by RGB features. In this design, depth features are not simply parallel to RGB features; instead, they interact and fuse meaningfully with RGB features through the attention mechanism. To validate the effectiveness of this design, ablation studies were conducted, and the network structure is as shown in Fig. 13. As shown in Table 8, the RGBD configuration achieves satisfactory performance across all metrics, with an accuracy of 95.8 % and an F1- score of 95.8 %, whereas the reversed DRGB variant exhibits a notable performance drop (accuracy: 92.2 %, F1-score: 92.0 %). The perfor- mance gap highlights a critical insight into modality prioritization in CA design: employing RGB features as queries yields more effective attention guidance than the reversed configuration. RGB images in- herently encapsulate rich semantic cues — such as color gradients, stress-induced discoloration, and textural variations — that are highly discriminative for fine-grained stress level classification. In contrast, depth data, while useful for conveying structural geometry and spatial morphology, lack the visual semantics necessary for precise query formulation. When RGB features serve as queries and depth features act as keys and values (RGBD configuration), the network learns to attend selectively to spatial regions where depth cues reinforce or contextual- ize color-based anomalies. Conversely, using depth as the query (DRGB configuration) introduces semantic misalignment, as low-level geomet- ric features struggle to effectively interrogate high-level appearance features in the RGB modality. This misdirection compromises feature integration and degrades classification accuracy, underscoring the im- portance of modality-aware role assignment in cross-modal attention mechanisms. This finding underscores the importance of query–key asymmetry in multimodal attention design. Assigning semantically richer features (e.g., RGB) as the query source enhances the network’s capacity to ex- tract context-aware correlations from auxiliary modalities (e.g., depth). This improves robustness and generalization in seedling stress classifi- cation tasks. 4. Limitations and future work The CNN–Transformer-based algorithm was proposed in this study for the classification of seedling stress levels, incorporating a lightweight CA mechanism to enable efficient fusion of RGBD multimodal data. Although the proposed method demonstrated competitive performance in terms of classification accuracy, real-time processing, and embedded deployment, several limitations remain that warrant further investiga- tion for broader applicability and technical advancement. The model’s generalization capacity is limited by the scale and di- versity of the current training dataset, which primarily includes a single crop species (bell pepper) under standardized stress conditions with limited variability in seedling age and environmental context. Such a narrow distribution raises concerns about domain shift, potentially leading to performance degradation when applied to other crop types, natural field environments, or multi-source stress factors. Future work should therefore focus on constructing a more representative RGBD dataset encompassing multiple crop species, growth stages, and diverse 14 Y. Zheng et al. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 247 (2026) 111710 environmental settings to improve the robustness and generalizability of the model in real-world scenarios. Although the model has been designed with lightweight components for edge deployment, further optimization is feasible and necessary. Advanced model compression techniques such as pruning and quan- tization, along with efficient convolutional architectures (e.g., depth- wise separable convolutions), could be employed to reduce inference latency and computational cost. Moreover, leveraging dedicated hard- ware accelerators such as neural processing units (NPU) would facili- tate real-time and energy-efficient inference, thereby lowering the prac- tical deployment threshold and enhancing applicability in agricultural equipment with limited resources. In summary, future research should focus on improving data diver- sity, developing automated and integrated preprocessing workflows, optimizing network efficiency through model compression, enhanc- ing cross-scenario generalization, and ensuring adaptability to hard- ware deployment. These advancements could facilitate practical imple- mentation and scalability of the proposed visual system in intelligent agriculture applications. 5. Conclusion In this study, a lightweight CNN–Transformer framework was devel- oped to assess seedling stress in real time during robotic transplanting by integrating color texture and depth geometry through a dual-stream CA strategy. The network employs a multi-scale tokenizer for rapid feature extraction, transformer encoders for long-range context, and attention pooling for compact classification. Model performance was evaluated on a dedicated RGBD dataset comprising seedlings subjected to graduated water-nutrient stress treatments and was benchmarked against several compact vision networks as well as a channel-stacking baseline. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed RGBD- CTA-F model achieves an overall classification accuracy of 95.8 % on a six-level stress dataset, while sustaining a real-time inference speed of 5.2 FPS. Qualitative and statistical comparisons showed that the proposed architecture delivered the most reliable stress-level pre- dictions while keeping computational requirements within the lim- its of an embedded Jetson platform. Future work will incorporate model compression for ultra-low-power devices and cross-crop valida- tion throughout the leafy growth period, thereby enabling continuous vitality monitoring and more responsive nursery management. Timely selection of high-quality seedlings during robotic transplanting is crucial for ensuring optimal crop
growth and productivity. However, accurate real-time seedling grading is technically challenging due to subtle
visual differences among stress levels and the limited computational capacity of edge devices. To address this,
we propose a lightweight RGBD (RGB and depth) multimodal framework for six-level stress classification of bell
pepper seedlings. Our approach integrates a dual-stream CNN–Transformer architecture in which hierarchical
cross-attention modules fuse color-texture cues from the RGB stream with depth-derived geometric cues at both
shallow and deep feature layers. The compact tokenizer rapidly extracts multi-scale fused features, which allow
transformer encoders to capture long-range dependencies, and an attention-pooling head produces class logits.
To validate our algorithm, a dedicated dataset of 1537 paired RGBD images was collected with an oblique-view
sensor during the pick-and-place cycle. Deployed on an edge-device, the network achieves an overall accuracy
of 95.8 % and maintains 5.2 frames per second when integrated into the parallel transplant-control pipeline.
Ablation studies reveal that effective fusion of RGBD channel can improve accuracy by 4.9 % over RGB-only
baseline model, which supports the effectiveness of the modality-aware design. This study integrates RGBD
imaging with an edge-ready hybrid network to provide a practical tool for automated seedling transplanting
and an effective solution for multimodal perception in precision agriculture.

With the rapid development of deep learning, especially the ad-
vent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), significant progress
has been made in the detection of seedling quality status. CNNs, by
increasing the depth of the network and applying various convolu-
tional operations, can hierarchically represent data. This capability
makes CNNs particularly well-suited for learning local features and
hierarchical representations in images (Alzubaidi et al., 2021). In di-
verse agricultural applications, several classic CNN-based models have
been extensively employed for disease classification and quality assess-
ment (Samiei et al., 2020). However, CNN architectures struggle to
capture long-range dependencies and the global structure of images.
When processing images with scattered features, it is difficult for CNNs
to effectively identify global context and spatial relationships. Further-
more, CNNs often involve a large number of parameters, particularly
in deeper networks (Alzubaidi et al., 2021).

In recent years, vision transformers have emerged as a promising
alternative that can improve accuracy and learning capabilities. These
models represent a shift from traditional CNN methods and focus on
capturing global context and relationships within image data (Han
et al., 2023). Building on this foundation, many high-performing mod-
els, such as swin transformer (Liu et al., 2021), have been proposed and
have achieved excellent performance in various computer vision tasks.
However, despite their improved accuracy, transformer-based image
recognition models still have the drawbacks of being computationally
extensive and architecturally complex. For small datasets, transformer
architectures perform poorly in the absence of multi-scale feature maps
and robust local feature extraction capabilities (Han et al., 2023).

Accumulated literature evidence indicates that RGB-based appro-
aches have achieved notable advances; nevertheless, their single-modal
nature inherently limits the information captured, restricting mod-
els from representing comprehensive plant traits (D. Li et al., 2020).
Regarding the assessment of seedling quality, analyzing RGB images
of seedlings can help determine their health status. Healthy plants
typically exhibit vibrant green colors, while unhealthy or disease-
affected plants appear yellowish or have spots (Agarwal and Dutta
Gupta, 2018). In addition, depth information can provide valuable
scale cues for analyzing the 3D structure of plants, including leaf size,
shape, and overall plant morphology, which are equally important
for assessing seedling quality (Z. Li et al., 2020). Multimodal data
exhibits both complementarity and consistency, allowing the modalities
to compensate for each other’s limitations and deficiencies. As a re-
sult, the perception and interpretation of multimodal information have
become a prominent research focus. For example, Sun et al. (2022) pro-
posed an attention-based fusion module to effectively integrate RGBD
(RGB+depth) information, mitigating the adverse effects of depth noise,
and significantly improving detection accuracy. In Xu et al. (2021), a
novel approach was introduced in which single-channel depth images
were re-encoded into three-channel images resembling RGB structures.

While recent progress in plant phenotyping and vision-based classi-
fication has significantly advanced the field, many existing approaches
remain constrained by their reliance on unimodal data sources. In
particular, they often use RGB imagery or vegetation indices derived
from limited spectral bands. These methods primarily focus on ob-
servable surface characteristics such as color intensity, leaf area, plant
height, or chlorophyll content. Although such features provide valuable
visual cues, they not fully capture subtle physiological stress indicators
or underlying morphological traits that are critical for determining
transplant readiness from an agronomic perspective. Moreover, such
parameters are often insufficient to detect early-stage physiological
stress, structural anomalies, or internal health conditions that are vital
for predicting post-transplant survival. Furthermore, these systems gen-
erally lack the capacity to jointly model surface texture and volumetric
cues, which are essential for evaluating key morphological indicators
such as seedling compactness, leaf curling, stem straightness, and root-
substrate integration. In automated transplanting scenarios, robotic
grippers must rapidly manipulate and assess individual seedlings with
sub-second latency. Consequently, classification models must operate
with real-time responsiveness and detect subtle quality variations that
are often imperceptible in 2D RGB imagery. While hyperspectral imag-
ing and full-resolution 3D reconstruction offer rich phenotypic detail,
their high equipment costs and computational demands render them
impractical for deployment on memory- and power-constrained edge
devices. It is beneficial to have a lightweight, multimodal classification
framework capable of real-time operation on low-power platforms, with
robust cross-modal feature representation and fusion capabilities.

"

In response to the practical demands of real-time seedling assess-
ment in automated transplanting systems, we present a task-specific
visual classification framework that leverages a CNN–Transformer hy-
brid architecture to fuse RGB and depth modalities. Our approach is
specifically designed to operate under the constraints of an edge-ready
embedded platform, enabling accurate, efficient, and real-time evalua-
tion of seedling stress conditions during robotic handling. The specific
objectives of this study are as follows: (1) To curate a novel stress-level
dataset for bell pepper seedlings, capturing both RGB and depth images
in real-time during the seedling transplantation process; (2) To develop
an optimized CNN–Transformer hybrid architecture that synergistically
combines convolutional feature extraction and attention mechanisms
to enhance training efficiency, improve predictive performance, and
enables computational efficiency suitable for deployment on resource-
constrained edge-device in agricultural environments; and (3) To pro-
pose a lightweight cross-attention (CA) multimodal fusion module that
effectively integrates RGBD data, significantly improving classification

We used the plug tray method for seedling cultivation, specifically
employing 36-hole trays filled with coconut coir—a widely used soilless
substrate known for its good air permeability and water retention.
The seedlings were grown following standard cultivation procedures.
The cultivation environment was maintained in an indoor incubator
with a controlled temperature of 27 ◦C, relative humidity set at 70 %,
and 15 h of simulated daylight provided each day. The water supply
regimen was adjusted according to growth stages: 1 L per application
during the early stage (0–15 days), 1.5 L during the mid-stage (15-30
days), and 2 L during the late stage (30–45 days). The nutrient solution
was prepared using a water-soluble nitrogen–phosphorus–potassium
compound fertilizer (20–20–20). During the early stage (0–15 days),
seedlings were irrigated with a 0.25 g/L solution (i.e., 1/4 strength).
From day 15 onward, the concentration was increased to 1.0 g/L (full
strength).

for fine-grained feature extraction and robust multimodal fusion to

The tokenizer is responsible for rapidly extracting rich feature maps
from the input RGB images using the CRP (Convolutional, ReLU, Pool-
ing) module. Subsequently, to adapt to the transformer module, the
feature maps are flattened into one-dimensional vectors and encoded
with positional embeddings. This step allows the model to focus on
local information at different positions within the feature maps. The
classifier receives the one-dimensional feature vectors with positional
embeddings and passes them through the transformer encoder module
to extract deep-level local and global information about the seedlings.
The output is further refined using the attention pooling module and
then classified using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP).

The input to the classification module comprises a sequence of fea-
ture vectors output by the tokenizer module, where each vector encodes
a distinct local region from the original RGB input. This sequence is
represented as a tensor of dimensions 196 × 256, corresponding to 196
spatial tokens, each with a feature dimensionality of 256. To retain
spatial structural information, a sinusoidal positional encoding strategy
is applied. This technique assigns a unique position-aware embedding
to each token based on its index in the sequence. By incorporating
these embeddings, the model can capture not only the semantic content
of each region but also their relative spatial arrangement, thereby
enabling more contextually aware classification.

RGBD images combine the color, texture, and shape information
from RGB images with the 3D structural information from depth im-
ages, providing a comprehensive visual representation that enables
the model to understand the scene’s content more comprehensively.
The details captured by RGB images help the model visually iden-
tify different objects, while depth information enhances the model’s
understanding of the spatial position and shape of objects. This data
fusion is particularly beneficial for improving the model’s robustness
under complex environmental conditions, such as changing lighting,
occlusion, and visual noise (Garbouge et al., 2021).

Multimodal data fusion can occur at different levels, including the
data level, feature level, and decision level (Sanchez-Riera et al., 2016).
Data-level fusion treats different types of data as indistinguishable
multi-channel inputs that are directly stacked at the model’s input
layer. Feature-level fusion considers the interrelationship between dif-
ferent modal data in the model’s intermediate layers. Decision-level
fusion independently processes each modal data at the model’s output
stage and then combines the results.

Due to the significant size variations among seedlings, multi-scale
fusion was introduced when designing the CA channels. The concept
of multi-scale representation has been validated (Li and Wu, 2024).
Low-level feature maps have smaller receptive fields and larger scales,
containing less semantic information and more low-level feature in-
formation, such as edges and colors. High-level feature maps contain
more semantic information and advanced feature information, such
as parts and overall structures of objects. CA channels leverage the
advantages of different receptive fields to fuse RGBD information,
allowing the network to adapt well to various multi-scale targets and
improve classification accuracy.

one for depth image features and the other for RGB image features.
These features are convolutional feature maps with the same spatial
dimensions to facilitate CA calculations. A query–key–value mechanism
is employed where RGB features serve as the query and depth features
as key and value. The dot product between query and key is calculated,

representation. Finally, the output of the CA is summed with the RGB
features to achieve fusion, as follows:

The training process was configured with a batch size of 32 and
an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4, which was scheduled using cosine
annealing with a minimum threshold of 1×10−5. The optimizer adopted
was AdamW, incorporating a weight decay coefficient of 6 × 10−2. To
stabilize convergence, a learning rate warm-up strategy was applied
over the first 10 epochs starting from 1 × 10−6, followed by 10 epochs
of cooling and a total training duration of 200 epochs. Label smoothing
with a smoothing factor of 0.1 was applied to mitigate overfitting and
enhance model generalization. Additionally, automatic mixed precision
was enabled to accelerate training and reduce memory consumption
without compromising numerical stability.

To obtain a reliable estimate of generalization performance under
limited data, we adopted an 80 %/20 % hold–out strategy combined
with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion. Specif-
ically, 20 % of the entire RGBD dataset was sequestered as an unseen
test set and accessed only once for the final evaluation reported. The
remaining 80 % was partitioned into five stratified folds that preserve
the original class distribution. For each cross-validation iteration, four
folds (≈ 64 % of the complete data) were used to train the network,
and the remaining fold (≈ 16 %) served as a validation set for early
stopping and hyper-parameter selection. All data splits were generated
with a fixed random state to ensure reproducibility.

The performance metrics in Table 3 reveal the relative strengths of
the three fusion strategies in terms of both overall correctness and class-
level discriminability. RGB-CTA sets the baseline with a balanced yet
restricted performance across all four metrics. This outcome reflects the
information bottleneck that is intrinsically present in the single-modal
RGB representation when differentiating subtle stress variations. The
marginal improvements of RGBD-CTA-D over RGB-CTA indicate that
simply appending depth as an extra channel offers limited complemen-
tary signals. It gives some noise reduction or contextual help but lacks
an explicit way to integrate modality-specific semantics. In comparison
with the baseline model, RGBD-CTA-F achieves approximately 5 %
improvements in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These en-
hancements serve to validate the effectiveness of cross-attention-based
feature-level fusion. By leveraging the complementary cues of RGB
appearance and depth geometry, the network can more dependably dis-
tinguish subtle seedling stress patterns (Sun et al., 2022). The consistent
precision and recall improvement indicates that RGBD-CTA-F enhances
positive identification accuracy. It also improves the comprehensive-
ness of detecting stressed classes, thereby increasing the F1-Score. It is
crucial for fine-grained multiclass stress classification where both false
positives and false negatives carry operational cost.

ble 3 reveals critical trade-offs between model complexity and perfor-
mance. The RGB-CTA and RGBD-CTA-D models exhibit nearly identical
parameter sizes (18.09 M vs. 18.35 M) and inference speeds (7.6 FPS
vs. 7.4 FPS), reflecting their shared backbone architecture with only
minor modifications to accommodate the depth channel. This finding
indicates that merely adding depth as an additional input dimension
incurs only a negligible computational burden. However, it also results
in only minimal improvements in classification accuracy (from 90.9 %
to 91.2 %). This observation underscores the restricted effectiveness of
data-level fusion in harnessing multimodal synergy.

From a computational perspective, giga floating-point operations
(GFLOPs) provide a more direct measure of workload than parameter
count alone. The GFLOPs increase from 8.2 (RGB-CTA) to 8.6 (RGBD-
CTA-D) and further to 10.3 (RGBD-CTA-F). This trend is consistent
with the architectural evolution from a single-stream backbone to a
dual-stream design with cross-attention-based feature fusion. While
RGBD-CTA-D introduces only a minor increase in computation by ex-
panding the input channel, RGBD-CTA-F incorporates parallel RGB and
depth encoders as well as cross-attention operations, which substan-
tially increase matrix multiplications and memory access operations.
The observed decrease in FPS is therefore primarily attributed to the
higher computational complexity and increased memory bandwidth
demand. In particular, cross-attention modules introduce additional
tensor reshaping and attention score computation.

The RGBD-CTA-D fusion approach treats depth and color equally,
without according precedence to modality-specific semantics or dy-
namic relevance. A more detailed analysis of the confusion matrix
reveals that, compared with the RGB-CTA baseline, the variety of
error types has increased, as shown in Fig. 9b. Consequently, this
approach results in information dilution rather than augmentation.
Specifically, several intermediate stress categories (such as W2N0-
W4N0) exhibit more frequent cross-class confusions. This implies that
the incorporated depth channel introduces ambiguities that cannot be
effectively resolved by simple concatenation. This discovery suggests
that naive data-level fusion may inadvertently intensify subtle inter-
class overlaps when the modalities are not adaptively coordinated.
Thus, it underscores the need for more structured fusion mechanisms
to clarify correlated yet distinct stress signatures.

A closer examination of the confusion matrices indicates that most
misclassified samples are concentrated in intermediate stress cate-
gories, such as W2N0, W4N4, and W4N0, where visual differences are
subtle and class boundaries are inherently ambiguous. These hard-to-
classify samples often share similar phenotypic characteristics, includ-
ing slight chlorosis, moderate leaf shrinkage, and comparable canopy
structure, making discrimination particularly challenging. In addition,
variations in observation angle may cause partial leaf self-occlusion
and canopy structure changes, occasionally masking discriminative
symptoms such as localized chlorosis or wilted leaves. Moreover,
forward–backward tilting of seedlings during robotic grasping can alter
the camera-to-seedling distance, introducing inconsistencies in appar-
ent scale that further increase classification ambiguity. RGBD-CTA-F
reduces these confusions more effectively under occlusion and scale
variation, indicating that cross-attention-based RGBD fusion improves
robustness by jointly leveraging appearance and geometric cues.

source lightweight classification networks in our dataset. The goal
of these experiments is to evaluate the deployment potential of our
method on resource-constrained embedded devices, emphasizing both
model size and classification accuracy. We chose models with parame-
ter counts not exceeding 50 M to reflect the practical need for a balance
between performance and compactness. The models were chosen to

ual architectures, and transformer-derived models). A suitable model
for real-world use must deliver high accuracy while remaining small
enough to run efficiently on diverse edge platforms.

The classifier part of the proposed method utilizes the attention
pooling module, which is an effective mechanism for enhancing the
model’s ability to process long sequential data. Attention pooling can
aggregate information from the input sequence, providing a com-
pressed information representation. It is particularly important for
dealing with limited attention spans. To validate the efficacy of this
design, in this section, ablation studies are carried out on the prediction
module. Specifically, the attention pooling module is removed from the
classifier section, and the variations in the model’s performance are
meticulously observed.

To rigorously evaluate the impact of feature fusion hierarchy in
the tokenizer, we designed four ablation variants (tokenizer I–IV) with
progressively reduced fusion complexity, as illustrated in Fig. 12. Tok-
enizer I (Fig. 12a) integrates both shallow and deep-level RGBD features
via CA modules, enabling multi-scale fusion. Tokenizer II and III ablate
shallow and deep fusion paths respectively, while tokenizer IV serves as
a fusion-free baseline. All the ablation models are guaranteed to have
an output of 14 × 14 × 256 through a 1 × 1 linear projection, ensuring
consistency with the input interface of the complete model.

In the design of the CA module, we selected RGB features as
the query (primary feature) and depth features as the key and value
(reference features). This is a common and effective design pattern in
multimodal learning. This pattern allows the model to leverage depth
features to enhance and complement the information provided by RGB
features. In this design, depth features are not simply parallel to RGB
features; instead, they interact and fuse meaningfully with RGB features
through the attention mechanism. To validate the effectiveness of this
design, ablation studies were conducted, and the network structure is
as shown in Fig. 13.

depth data, while useful for conveying structural geometry and spatial
morphology, lack the visual semantics necessary for precise query
formulation. When RGB features serve as queries and depth features act
as keys and values (RGBD configuration), the network learns to attend
selectively to spatial regions where depth cues reinforce or contextual-
ize color-based anomalies. Conversely, using depth as the query (DRGB
configuration) introduces semantic misalignment, as low-level geomet-
ric features struggle to effectively interrogate high-level appearance
features in the RGB modality. This misdirection compromises feature
integration and degrades classification accuracy, underscoring the im-
portance of modality-aware role assignment in cross-modal attention
mechanisms.

In this study, a lightweight CNN–Transformer framework was devel-
oped to assess seedling stress in real time during robotic transplanting
by integrating color texture and depth geometry through a dual-stream
CA strategy. The network employs a multi-scale tokenizer for rapid
feature extraction, transformer encoders for long-range context, and
attention pooling for compact classification. Model performance was
evaluated on a dedicated RGBD dataset comprising seedlings subjected
to graduated water-nutrient stress treatments and was benchmarked
against several compact vision networks as well as a channel-stacking
baseline. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed RGBD-
CTA-F model achieves an overall classification accuracy of 95.8 %
on a six-level stress dataset, while sustaining a real-time inference
speed of 5.2 FPS. Qualitative and statistical comparisons showed that
the proposed architecture delivered the most reliable stress-level pre-
dictions while keeping computational requirements within the lim-
its of an embedded Jetson platform. Future work will incorporate
model compression for ultra-low-power devices and cross-crop valida-
tion throughout the leafy growth period, thereby enabling continuous
vitality monitoring and more responsive nursery management.
